title: Prior Art Check: AIMD-Style TTL Control Outside LLM Agents
layman_summary: We searched CDN, database, DNS, and browser caching literature to see if anyone already used a TCP-style additive-growth/multiplicative-cut rule to adjust how long cached data stays valid, and found the idea is close to novel but not perfectly so.
summary: This research artifact closes the paper's remaining novelty gap around AIMD-for-cache-TTL by systematically searching CDN, database/materialized-view, DNS, and browser/HTTP caching literature (scholarly + general web search across ~9 query angles) for prior work applying a literal additive-increase/multiplicative-decrease control law to cache TTL, freshness, or expiration outside the LLM-agent setting. It confirms and precisely characterizes the two near-hits already flagged during planning -- ClepsydraCache (Thoma et al., USENIX Security 2023, arXiv:2104.11469), whose authors themselves state their TTL-reduction-rate schedule 'is comparable to TCP congestion control [RFC 2581]', and Vincent Cate's 1992 Alex filesystem / RFC 7234 heuristic-freshness age-proportional TTL -- and discovers ONE new, more directly relevant hit not in the original plan: Concur (Chen et al., ICML 2025, arXiv:2601.22705), which applies a genuine two-sided AIMD rule INSIDE an LLM-agent inference-serving setting, but to admission control of concurrent agents gated on KV-cache pressure/hit-rate signals, not to any object's TTL or content-staleness. It also confirms d-TTL/f-TTL (Basu et al., SIGMETRICS 2017, arXiv:1704.04448) and FreshCache (Mansoor et al., arXiv:2607.04281) use non-AIMD control laws (Robbins-Monro stochastic approximation targeting a hit rate; a fitted probabilistic staleness gate, respectively) via direct full-text grep, finding zero occurrences of AIMD/additive/multiplicative/congestion/TCP terms in d-TTL's text. No hit was found in database materialized-view refresh, DNS TTL, or browser/HTTP caching literature describing a literal loss-event-triggered AIMD rule for freshness/TTL. The deliverable is a citation-backed Related Work paragraph (in research_report.md) that narrows the paper's novelty claim precisely: no prior work applies AIMD to a per-object/per-call-site TTL triggered by confirmed content staleness in ANY caching domain surveyed, and the one genuine within-agent-setting AIMD precedent (Concur) targets a categorically different variable (concurrency admission, not freshness), which should be added to the paper's Related Work and its comparison table as a 'same-mechanism-different-target' distinction, not a competing baseline.
answer:
SEARCH SCOPE AND SUMMARY OF WHAT WAS AND WAS NOT FOUND. We ran nine query angles across scholarly-mode and general-mode search (CDN/AIMD-TTL phrasing, database materialized-view refresh, DNS TTL, browser/HTTP cache staleness, ACM/IEEE site-restricted search, Robbins-Monro/stochastic-approximation TTL, and the two leads already surfaced during planning: ClepsydraCache and Cate's Alex/RFC 7234), followed by full-text grep on the two most load-bearing candidate PDFs. Outside the LLM-agent setting, no work was found in the CDN, database/materialized-view, DNS, or browser/HTTP caching literature that applies a genuine two-sided additive-increase/multiplicative-decrease (AIMD) control law -- small additive growth on a 'good' outcome, sharp multiplicative cut on a specific 'bad' outcome -- to an object's time-to-live, freshness, or expiration [1, 2, 6]. One new and directly relevant hit surfaced that was NOT anticipated in the original research plan: Concur (Chen et al., ICML 2025) applies AIMD inside an LLM-agentic inference-serving system, but to a different control variable entirely [3].

CANDIDATE 1 -- ClepsydraCache (Thoma, Niesler, Funke, Leander, Mayr, Pohl, Davi, Gueneysu; USENIX Security 2023; arXiv:2104.11469). This is the closest true near-hit and was verified by direct full-text grep of the arXiv PDF, not a secondary summary. The mechanism is exactly as previously flagged from the UMass CS677 lecture note, and the paper's own text confirms the framing in the authors' words: 'we approximate the desired behavior by dynamically adapting R_TTL based on experienced conflicts. The approach is comparable to TCP congestion control [2]', where reference [2] is Allman/Paxson/Stevens, 'TCP congestion control', RFC 2581, 1999 [1]. The control shape is a global TTL-reduction-rate R_TTL that starts at an initial value and decays slowly toward a minimum (increasing effective cache-entry lifetime, i.e. the 'growth' phase) until a conflict -- a cache miss landing on a dynamic set with no free entry -- triggers a sharp increase in R_TTL (a 'shark-fin shaped evolution', per the paper's own Figure 3), which is the AIMD-shaped decrease phase applied to eviction aggressiveness rather than to TTL length directly [1]. Three properties distinguish it decisively from this paper's hypothesis: (a) the 'bad event' triggering the multiplicative response is a security side-channel conflict signal (an address-collision on a hardware dynamic set), not confirmed content incorrectness or staleness; (b) the adaptation is applied GLOBALLY across the entire cache (one shared R_TTL for all entries), not per-object or per-call-site; (c) the domain is CPU cache micro-architectural security (mitigating Prime+Probe/Flush+Reload side-channel attacks), unrelated to content freshness, CDNs, databases, or LLM agents. ClepsydraCache is genuinely AIMD-adjacent by the authors' own characterization, but it targets a categorically different trigger, granularity, and problem domain than a confirmed-staleness-triggered per-call-site TTL rule.

CANDIDATE 2 -- Concur (Chen, Ye, Tang, Sun, Tian, Wang, Li, Wen, Han, Zhang; ICML 2025; arXiv:2601.22705), 'Proactive Agent-Level Admission Control for Efficient Agentic Batch Inference'. This is a NEW finding beyond the original research plan and is arguably the single most important discovery of this search, because it IS set inside LLM-agent inference serving. Concur treats the number of concurrently admitted agents W_t as a TCP-style 'congestion window': it additively increases W_t by a constant factor when KV-cache pressure U_t stays below a low threshold, and multiplicatively cuts W_t (by a factor beta) when BOTH cache pressure is high (U_t > U_high) AND the cache hit rate falls below a threshold (H_t < H_thresh), explicitly to prevent 'middle-phase thrashing' from cascading KV-cache evictions [3]. This confirms AIMD has already reached the LLM-agent-serving literature, but the controlled variable is agent-level admission/concurrency, not any single object's or tool-call's time-to-live -- Concur never adapts a per-key TTL, freshness window, or staleness threshold; its 'decrease' event is a systemic capacity-pressure signal (aggregate cache hit-rate degradation), not a per-object confirmed-stale read. It is the closest work in spirit (AIMD + LLM agents + caching) but orthogonal in mechanism (capacity control vs. freshness control) to a confirmed-staleness-triggered per-call-site TTL rule, and should be cited explicitly as evidence that AIMD is a live idea in this exact research community, strengthening rather than undermining the paper's positioning.

CANDIDATE 3/4 -- d-TTL / f-TTL (Basu, Sundarrajan, Ghaderi, Shakkottai, Sitaraman; SIGMETRICS 2017; arXiv:1704.04448) and FreshCache (Mansoor, Ahmad, Yoon; arXiv:2607.04281, ICML 2026 Oral, titled 'Risk-Constrained Freshness-Aware Semantic Caching for Open-Web Retrieval-Augmented LLMs'). Full-text grep of the d-TTL PDF for AIMD/additive/multiplicative/congestion/TCP returned zero matches [2], confirming the paper's own related-work section does not cite or reference any AIMD-style prior art -- d-TTL's update rule increments its TTL parameter theta by a fixed step eta*h* on every cache miss and decrements it by eta*(1-h*) on every cache hit, which is a stochastic-approximation (Robbins-Monro) rule converging to a target hit rate, not a loss-event-triggered AIMD rule with an asymmetric large-cut response to a specific bad event [2]. FreshCache independently confirmed via search summary and its own abstract framing (a 'risk-constrained' fitted probabilistic staleness gate for open-web RAG) uses a fitted/calibrated gating threshold rather than any additive/multiplicative feedback-control update law [4]. Both are correctly characterized in the paper as non-AIMD comparators, and this search found no reason to revise that.

CANDIDATE 5 -- Cate's Alex global filesystem (USENIX File Systems Workshop, Ann Arbor, May 1992) and its descendant, RFC 7234 Section 4.2.2 heuristic freshness [6]. Alex provided transparent read access to anonymous-FTP Internet files and used 'special caching algorithms that take into account the properties of the files and of the network' with per-file relaxed consistency, and its age-proportional heuristic ('cache duration as a percentage of file age, commonly 10% of time since Last-Modified') was later codified into HTTP caching practice and is explicitly named in RFC 7234 and implemented by browsers including Chrome [5, 6]. This IS the most-cited 'adaptive TTL' idiom in web caching folklore, and it does adapt TTL as a function of observed data (the file's own age) -- but it has no loss-event feedback loop at all: there is no 'bad outcome' that triggers a cut, no growth phase reacting to 'good' outcomes, and no asymmetric response shape. It is proportional-to-age control, not AIMD, and this distinction must be stated explicitly in the paper so a reviewer does not mistake heuristic freshness for a missed AIMD citation.

DOMAINS WITH NO HIT. Database/materialized-view refresh: search surfaced budget-aware and performance-benefit-driven refresh scheduling (e.g. StarRocks partition-TTL properties, budget-constrained refresh policies), but none described as congestion-control- or AIMD-inspired, and no academic paper combining 'congestion control' framing with materialized-view refresh scheduling was found [7]. DNS TTL adaptation: no AIMD-specific DNS caching paper was found; DNS TTL literature remains dominated by static/negative-caching and prefetch-based adaptation, not loss-event AIMD. Browser/HTTP caching: search returned only the RFC 7234 heuristic-freshness mechanism above and stale-while-revalidate/stale-if-error soft-TTL directives, neither of which is AIMD-shaped.

CONCLUSION AND PRECISE NOVELTY CLAIM. In the sources surveyed, no prior work -- inside or outside the LLM-agent setting -- applies a literal confirmed-staleness-triggered AIMD control law to a per-object or per-call-site cache TTL/freshness window. The two clearest non-agent AIMD-TTL precedents both target different triggers and granularities than confirmed staleness: ClepsydraCache's AIMD-shaped reduction-rate schedule reacts to a global security side-channel conflict signal, not per-object correctness [1]; Cate/RFC 7234's age-proportional heuristic has no loss-event feedback at all [5, 6]. Within the LLM-agent setting specifically, Concur (ICML 2025) establishes that AIMD is already a known control pattern in this literature, but for agent admission/concurrency, never for object-level TTL or freshness [3]. To the authors' knowledge, as of this search (August 2026), this is the first work to apply a confirmed-staleness-triggered AIMD control law to a per-call-site cache TTL, in the LLM-agent setting or otherwise -- a narrower and more defensible claim than 'novel only within the agent setting', since the search found no non-agent prior either. The paper's Related Work should therefore (a) cite ClepsydraCache and Cate/RFC-7234 as AIMD-adjacent and age-proportional non-agent TTL precedents respectively, explicitly distinguished by trigger; and (b) add Concur as the closest AIMD-in-LLM-agents precedent, explicitly distinguished by controlled variable (concurrency vs. freshness) -- strengthening, not weakening, the paper's positioning, since it shows the mechanism has independent traction in the target community without pre-empting this paper's specific application.

sources.title: ClepsydraCache -- Preventing Cache Attacks with Time-Based Evictions (Thoma et al., USENIX Security 2023)
sources.summary: Full-text-grepped PDF (arXiv:2104.11469). Authors explicitly state their global TTL-reduction-rate schedule 'is comparable to TCP congestion control [RFC 2581]', with slow decay of R_TTL between conflicts and a sharp increase upon a hardware cache-set conflict (a security side-channel signal, not content staleness); global not per-object; CPU-cache security domain, unrelated to content freshness/CDN/DB/agent caching.

sources.title: Adaptive TTL-Based Caching for Content Delivery (Basu, Sundarrajan, Ghaderi, Shakkottai, Sitaraman; SIGMETRICS 2017)
sources.summary: Full-text-grepped PDF (arXiv:1704.04448); zero matches for AIMD/additive/multiplicative/congestion/TCP. d-TTL uses a Robbins-Monro stochastic-approximation update (increment on miss, decrement on hit, both by fixed step sizes weighted by target hit rate h*) converging to a target hit rate -- confirmed non-AIMD, and the paper cites no AIMD/TCP-style prior art in its own related work.

sources.title: Concur: Proactive Agent-Level Admission Control for Efficient Agentic Batch Inference (Chen et al., ICML 2025)
sources.summary: New find, not anticipated in the original plan. Applies genuine two-sided AIMD (additive growth of admitted-agent count when cache pressure is low, multiplicative cut when pressure is high AND hit rate is low) inside an LLM-agent batch-inference serving system -- but the controlled variable is agent-level concurrency/admission, gated on aggregate KV-cache pressure and hit-rate signals, never a per-object TTL or per-call-site freshness window. Closest AIMD-in-LLM-agents precedent found; orthogonal target variable to this paper's hypothesis.

sources.title: Risk-Constrained Freshness-Aware Semantic Caching for Open-Web Retrieval-Augmented LLMs (Mansoor, Ahmad, Yoon; ICML 2026 Oral) -- 'FreshCache'
sources.summary: Confirmed via abstract/search summary as a risk-constrained, fitted probabilistic staleness gate for open-web RAG caching, not an additive/multiplicative feedback-control update law; already correctly positioned in the paper as a non-AIMD comparator.

sources.title: Vince Cate -- creator of the Alex global filesystem (USENIX File Systems Workshop, 1992)
sources.summary: Alex (1992) provided transparent caching read-access to anonymous-FTP Internet files with per-file relaxed consistency and file/network-property-aware caching; origin of the widely cited age-proportional ('percentage of file age') adaptive-TTL heuristic later codified in HTTP caching. No loss-event feedback loop -- proportional-to-age, not AIMD.

sources.title: RFC 7234: Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP/1.1): Caching, Section 4.2.2 (Heuristic Freshness)
sources.summary: Codifies the age-proportional heuristic freshness rule (commonly 10% of time since Last-Modified, as implemented by Chrome and other browsers) descending from Alex's approach; confirmed to be purely age-proportional with no additive-growth/multiplicative-cut feedback structure, distinguishing it explicitly from AIMD.

sources.title: [Negative-result domain search: database materialized-view refresh]
sources.summary: Searches for congestion-control-inspired or AIMD-style materialized-view refresh scheduling (QuestDB TTL-on-materialized-views, StarRocks partition-TTL/budget-aware refresh, PostgreSQL concurrent-refresh literature) surfaced budget- and performance-benefit-driven scheduling but no paper or system explicitly combining congestion-control/AIMD framing with materialized-view refresh; reported as a negative result, not evidence of absence.

follow_up_questions: Should the paper add Concur (ICML 2025, arXiv:2601.22705) as a positively-cited 'AIMD is already live in this exact research community' precedent in Related Work, and if so, does its admission-control mechanism suggest a natural extension (combining per-call-site staleness-triggered TTL AIMD with Concur-style admission-level AIMD in the same agent loop) worth flagging as future work?

The ClepsydraCache characterization here rests on one full-text-verified arXiv PDF (v2, revised Aug 2022) plus the paper's own RFC-2581 citation; the final published USENIX Security 2023 version was not independently diffed against the arXiv version for wording changes to the AIMD framing -- worth a quick page-vs-PDF sanity check before quoting the exact phrase in the paper.

The database/materialized-view and DNS-TTL negative results relied on general web search rather than a scholarly-mode systematic literature search of DB/networking venues (VLDB, SIGMOD, IMC, PAM); a dedicated scholarly-mode pass restricted to those venues would raise confidence in the 'no hit found' claim for those two domains specifically.
